spoken_segments.text: If you look at it, most AI product steps are bounded decisions and not generation problems.

So to give a couple of examples, user query intent classification, a ranker picking a suggestion out of N options, checking whether a citation is valid or not, routing to the correct model or expert, so on so forth.
Till now, we have been paying the full LLM cost and latency to get an answer to all these bounded problems.

spoken_segments.text: Jev at Glean fills the gap between general LLMs and fine-tuned classifiers.

Classification itself isn't a new problem, like people have been trying to solve it since forever. We can have multiple ways to solve it. Some of the things that we have tried out include using a general purpose LLM, using an open model something like Leya, fine-tuning that open model, or using Jev.

Now all these approaches and all these different ways have their pros and cons. With a general purpose LLM, we incur a lot of cost and latency, while with something like Jev we get no generated text output.

Another advantage that we have been seeing with Jev is that as the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again. We can just change our prompt a bit and make it work out of the box.

spoken_segments.text: Before we go into these individual problems, I want to touch upon how we evaluate these changes. Like we have a huge customer base having millions of users so we don't want any of the change that we make to regress our product.

We have a multiphase rollout approach to any change that we are making. This includes having a golden eval set for almost every possible thing, like any place where we have generative AI, any place where we have any form of intelligence involved, we have a golden eval set for that space.

We soak all of these changes for a significant amount of time for our internal use case, like we have around 1,500 people at Glean right now. We soak all of these changes within our Glean instance for like a couple of weeks, we get active feedback, we have a very active feedback loop from our internal users, we work upon that and then we go for an A/B testing with our customers.

spoken_segments.text: The first problem that we tried out with a decision model was query classification. Query classification is when we want to know the nature of user queries. This helps us realize what kind of jobs are people using Glean for—for example, if people are using more for sales-like queries, we focus more on that; if people are using more for engineering-type use cases, we focus more on that.

We tried out three different approaches over here, and this is data from our test bed. We used an open source Leya model, then we tried out Jev, and then we fine-tuned the Leya model on our own compute resources.
Jev is the best no-training option in our opinion. It nearly doubles the output quality of a base Leya model and is able to perform at a 90% quality in comparison to a fine-tuned Leya.

With Jev, we don't have to go through the very tedious process of data collection, data cleaning, incurring the cost for compute, training the model, fine-tuning the model again and again as the taxonomy changes. And at the same time, we don't have to worry about hosting the model or incurring the inference cost.

spoken_segments.text: The next problem we went to is expert routing. This is a pretty common problem statement in the industry right now. Like, hey, when the user query comes in, what expert do we route it to? How do we ensure that the response to the user is of the best possible quality?

The way we have been solving this is Glean receives the user query and then decides what's the best expert to answer the query. Till now we have been using a general purpose LLM to route to the correct expert.
We set up a testbed with N experts, and in our experiments found a significantly high precision when using Jev, and that too at an almost 8x reduction in latency.

We had to change our implementation or infrastructure significantly to integrate Jev into this specific stage of our product. But the reduction in latency justifies that inherent complexity in the system. We at Glean have been trying to build systems in the simplest possible manners. This is one of the rare pieces where we believe complexity is worth it.

spoken_segments.text: Next, I'll walk you through the ranker problem statement that I talked about. When we receive a user query, we also want to generate the best follow up suggestions for the user. This helps us in getting discoverability for our product and ensuring that the user has the best possible experience. We also want to recommend or say preempt what the next user query might be.

Internally we call this system Q, like Q as in the literal Q. The way this works, we have like 10 or 15 different sources that are generating suggestions independently of each other. These suggestions are generated by natural language LLMs, and it's like a proper natural language query. Once these suggestions are in, we have a ranking step. So the ranker takes in all these suggestions, takes in the first user query, takes in the output that Glean gave, and then all these suggestions in that context. The ranker is then asked to decide: hey, you have these suggestions, what do you think is the best one?

A pretty interesting bottleneck that we had over here is we want the response to be snappy. We cannot have a state where we give the textual response to the user and then wait 5 seconds for generating the follow up suggestion. That's why we have time limits on these suggestions. So right now this step had a time limit of 1.5 to 2 seconds.

Jev no doubt gave us a better quality and far better latency than what we had with the general purpose LLM. But two things stood out over there. First, we were able to give a suggestion within our time bounds in 99.2% cases. With the general purpose LLM, this was almost 90%. So this ensures that we have user engagement in far more user queries now.

The second thing is at Glean whenever we use these LLMs, we have guardrails in the sense that LLM might not be good at generating a response or might be making some specific kind of mistakes, so we have checks and balances for all those possible mistakes that we see. With a general purpose LLM, we were able to generate a valid suggestion in almost 90% of the cases—we still had some places where LLM was either generating a response in a different language or the output did not meet certain other criteria that we had written programmatically. With Jev, we found zero cases to be there when the output was invalid.

Now a natural question is like, hey, but you would have used a different prompt. Yes, the prompt was somewhat different, but we try to mimic the prompt in the two cases to the largest extent possible so that we don't have a divergence. Again, we at Glean want to keep the system as simple as possible.

spoken_segments.text: Another benefit we see with using a decision model is how we can control the thresholds. Because in this ranker problem statement we are getting specific probabilities of each output. We are not restricted to a binary yes or no response. We get like hey, these were the five options and these are the probabilities of these five options.

With this we are able to fine-tune the thresholds based on the deployment. We have put in self-learning systems which, based on the customer deployment and the nature of usage that the specific customer has, fine-tunes the thresholds by itself. This ensures that the experience in each and every customer out there is the best possible based on how they use Glean, not a general purpose solution that fits all.

scenes.alignment_note: 'specific probabilities of each output' maps to the confidence scores shown in Turn A (0.49, 0.30, 0.16, 0.05) and Turn B (0.67, 0.29, 0.04), while threshold tuning per customer deployment connects to the dashed cutoff line and bullet 2 ('config flag tuned per surface').

spoken_segments.text: Okay, this is an interesting one. Now moving on from how we have been making the experience of our end users better, we also tried using Jev in some other parts of our development pipeline. One of them was how we use LLM as judges. Like all of us have been using LLM as judges for quite some time now. There is an input, there is an output, and we use an LLM to judge how the quality of the output is. Now naturally, whenever we use LLM as a judge, we repeat the experiment multiple times to account for the variability in the response.

At Glean, we used Jev for a very specific part of our evaluation pipeline. Glean responses, like any other AI product out there, have citations. This is how people trust that Glean's answer was correct and it is grounded in the correct document. Now we hold these citations to a very high bar, and we have a specific part in our evaluation pipeline where we check whether the cited document really supports the claim made in the answer or not. This again seems to be a pretty simple yes or no question: whether the claim is supported or not.

With Jev, no doubt we had a far better latency and cost like visible in the slide over here. The interesting thing we noticed over here is how consistent and reproducible Jev results were in comparison to something like say Luna. In the 28 or 30 use cases that we had, only one run had a difference in response. Apart from that, everything was consistent.

What this ensures are two things for us as engineers or developers at Glean: we are not only improving the quality of our product in a linear fashion anymore. Any improvement of this extent in the development pipeline leads to an exponential increase in how we can improve the product. So if I as a developer am able to ship things like 5x faster—like this is a significant reduction in latency if I run this experiment across thousands and thousands of entries, this saves a lot of time. And again, I don't have to run the same input-output pair multiple times, because the results from Jev are quite consistent. So if I'm able to increase my own productivity by like 5x or 6x, I can ship 6x the features to our customers, and this happens across like 500 or 300 engineers at Glean. So the impact of a good decision model is no longer linear, it is exponential on how we can improve the product.

spoken_segments.text: Now moving on from product and LLMs as judges, this is a pretty important part of how we use our customer data. Like security is something that all our customers expect from us. So, for example, we have checks and balances on all the inputs and outputs coming from a tool, all the inputs and outputs from an LLM.

Till now, we at Glean have like a multiphase approach—there are two phases to this. The first one is like a recall-heavy phase and the second one is the final heavy-loaded LLM. All these calls are made in parallel to the actual tool input-output calls. Till now we used to host a virtual classifier using T4 GPUs across all our customers. So Glean is a single-tenant solution, like we don't use or share resources across customers, every customer gets its own deployment, gets its own instance, and gets all the resources. So assuming we have 1,000 customers out there, we had to maintain virtual classifiers across all these 1,000 customers, which becomes a pretty difficult problem statement in itself which takes up a lot of time from Glean engineers.

So looking at the results over here, the overall recall of the first phase where we used to have a virtual classifier—we replaced that with Jev—went from 31.5% to 90.2%. At the same time, we are seeing a significant reduction in cost. Now this cost is only the resource cost mentioned over here, but we are also saving cost on the engineering resources over here. We don't have to invest like two or three engineers who are full time maintaining those virtual classifiers or those T4 GPUs across customers. The improvement or the savings that we have are far more than 50%.

scenes.screen_title: A simple rule for when to reach for a decision model
scenes.visual_summary: Slide 15 presenting a three-row decision framework with blue question cards on the left branching into white/blue recommendation boxes on the right for choosing between generative models, Jev, fine-tuned classifiers, or a hybrid pattern.
ocr_details: A simple rule for when to reach for a decision model
Can the output be listed in advance? -> No -> keep a generative model (queries, explanations, tool arguments) | Yes -> benchmark Jev
Are labels stable and volume high? -> Yes -> also benchmark a fine-tuned classifier | No -> Jev's zero-shot flexibility pays off
Do you also need dynamic text? -> Go hybrid: Jev picks the tool, the LLM writes the arguments

spoken_segments.text: In conclusion, a simple rule that we have been using at Glean is: can the output be listed in advance? If no, then it's a freeform generative text problem statement—go back to something that can generate freeform text. If yes, then use Jev.

Are labels stable and volume high? If this is the case where the labels are stable, which is rarely the case anymore, you can also fine-tune a model. But if the labels change, which in my opinion is quite frequent these days, then again use something like Jev.
Obviously, if you need dynamic text, feel free to try out more hybrid approaches like Jev along with freeform text LLMs.
